[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance teaches product owners, business analysts, and engineers how to author well-formed BDD Gherkin `.feature` files that serve as executable specifications in the project's BDD lifecycle. It covers the `@FR-` requirement tagging convention, the concern abbreviation table, Gherkin syntax rules, scenario granularity, data conventions, and the operational workflow from draft to committed repository artifact.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- **Specification precision** — well-formed Gherkin scenarios eliminate ambiguity at the point of authoring, not downstream during implementation or QA
- **Agent readiness** — `.feature` files authored to these conventions are directly consumable as acceptance criteria in agent-executable task specs ([PTN-APP-GOV-006](../../../../patterns/application/governance/PTN-APP-GOV-006-bdd-scenario-agent-acceptance-criteria-pattern.md))
- **Polyglot consistency** — scenarios authored once drive automated tests across all supported languages (Python, C#, Java, Rust) with no per-language reinterpretation
- **Traceability** — the `@FR-` tagging convention creates a machine-readable link from every scenario to its parent requirement, enabling automated traceability reporting

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

The [BDD Lifecycle Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/bdd-lifecycle-strategy.md) establishes that Gherkin `.feature` files are the single source of truth for functional requirements. These files are authored before implementation begins and serve as executable acceptance criteria for both human engineers and AI agents. The quality of the `.feature` file directly determines the quality of the implementation — a vague or poorly tagged scenario produces vague or incorrect code.

This guidance fills the gap between the strategic vision (the white paper) and the operational conventions (the project's `docs/requirements/functional/README.md`). The white paper describes the lifecycle; this guidance describes how to write a good `.feature` file.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#success-criteria]

#### Success Criteria

- Product owners can author a conformant `.feature` file with AI assistance in under 30 minutes for a typical concern
- Every `@FR-` tag in the repository follows the `@FR-{CONCERN}-{FILE}-{NNN}` format
- No `.feature` file contains PHI, PII, or production data values
- All scenarios use the project's ubiquitous language from `docs/glossary.md`

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-1-understanding-the-feature-file-structure]

### Step 1: Understanding the Feature File Structure

A `.feature` file is a plain-text file written in Gherkin syntax. It lives at `docs/requirements/functional/<concern>/<file>.feature` (for `@FR-` functional specs) or `docs/requirements/non-functional/<concern>/<file>.feature` (for `@NFR-` behavioral non-functional specs) and describes the behavioral requirements for a single functional area or quality attribute.

**Minimum structure:**

```gherkin
@<concern-tag>
Feature: <Feature name>
  <Feature description — 1-3 sentences explaining the business capability>

  @FR-<CONCERN>-<FILE>-<NNN>
  Scenario: <Scenario name>
    Given <precondition>
    When <action>
    Then <expected outcome>
```

**Key elements:**

| Element | Purpose | Required |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Feature-level tag | Groups all scenarios by concern (e.g., `@clock`) | Yes |
| Feature keyword + name | Names the capability being specified | Yes |
| Feature description | Explains business context in plain language | Yes |
| `@FR-` tag | Uniquely identifies each scenario as a traceable requirement | Yes — on every Scenario and Scenario Outline |
| Scenario keyword + name | Names one observable behavior | Yes |
| Given/When/Then steps | Defines the precondition, action, and expected outcome | Yes |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-2-writing-the-feature-description]

### Step 2: Writing the Feature Description

The feature description appears immediately after the `Feature:` keyword line. It provides business context for anyone reading the file — product owners, engineers, or AI agents.

**Guidelines:**

- Write 1–3 sentences in plain business language
- Explain _why_ the capability exists, not _how_ it works internally
- Reference the relevant business domain, not implementation technology
- Use vocabulary from `docs/glossary.md`

**Good:**

```gherkin
Feature: Timezone-aware time conversion
  The platform operates across multiple US timezones. All timestamps displayed
  to users must reflect their configured timezone, with correct handling of
  Daylight Saving Time transitions.
```

**Bad:**

```gherkin
Feature: Timezone-aware time conversion
  Uses DateTimeOffset with TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById to convert
  UTC to IANA timezone identifiers stored in the user profile table.
```

The bad example describes implementation, not business intent. A product owner cannot validate whether `TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById` is the right approach — but they can validate whether "timestamps displayed to users must reflect their configured timezone" is the right requirement.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-3-assigning-fr--requirement-tags]

### Step 3: Assigning @FR- Requirement Tags

Every scenario and scenario outline must carry a unique requirement tag that identifies it as a traceable requirement. The tag format is:

```
@FR-{CONCERN}-{FILE}-{NNN}     (functional requirements)
@NFR-{CONCERN}-{FILE}-{NNN}    (behavioral non-functional requirements)
```

| Segment | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| `FR` or `NFR` | Fixed prefix — "Functional Requirement" or "Non-Functional Requirement" | `FR`, `NFR` |
| `{CONCERN}` | 2–4 character abbreviation from the concern abbreviation table | `CLK` |
| `{FILE}` | 1–4 character abbreviation identifying the `.feature` file within the concern | `TZ` |
| `{NNN}` | Three-digit sequence number, incrementing by 10 | `010`, `020`, `030` |

> **When to use `@NFR-` vs `@FR-`:** Use `@NFR-` when the scenario tests a quality attribute (security, resilience, performance boundary) that is behavioral and deterministic — testable at the unit/integration level. Use `@FR-` for functional business logic. See the BDD Lifecycle Strategy §5.0 for the full behavioral vs. systemic decision criteria. Systemic NFRs (load testing, chaos engineering) do not use BDD and are documented as `REQ-NFR-*.md` in `docs/requirements/non-functional/`.

**Why increment by 10?** Gap numbering reserves space for inserting new scenarios between existing ones without renumbering. If `@FR-CLK-TZ-010` and `@FR-CLK-TZ-020` exist and a new scenario needs to go between them, use `@FR-CLK-TZ-015`.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#concern-abbreviation-table]

#### Concern Abbreviation Table

The project maintains a concern abbreviation table in `docs/requirements/functional/README.md`. Each concern directory maps to a short code:

| Concern Directory | Abbreviation | Description |
|-------------------|--------------|-------------|
| `clock` | `CLK` | Time, timezone, DST handling |
| `configuration` | `CFG` | Application configuration, feature flags |
| `resilience` | `RST` | Retry, circuit breaker, timeout |
| `cache` | `CCH` | Cache read, write, invalidation, TTL |
| `validation` | `VLD` | Input validation, domain rules |
| `audit` | `AUD` | Audit event recording, compliance logging |
| `identity` | `IDN` | Authentication, authorization, user context |

**When you introduce a new concern**, add a row to this table in the project's `docs/requirements/functional/README.md` before creating the first `.feature` file. The abbreviation must be unique across the project, 2–4 uppercase characters, and mnemonic (recognizable without looking up the table).
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#file-abbreviation]

#### File Abbreviation

Within a concern, each `.feature` file gets its own abbreviation. Examples for the `clock` concern:

| File | Abbreviation | Full Tag Prefix |
|------|--------------|-----------------|
| `core.feature` | `CR` | `@FR-CLK-CR-` |
| `timezone.feature` | `TZ` | `@FR-CLK-TZ-` |
| `overrides.feature` | `OV` | `@FR-CLK-OV-` |

**Rules:**

- File abbreviations must be unique within their concern (not globally)
- 1–4 uppercase characters
- Document the mapping in a comment at the top of the `.feature` file or in the concern's directory-level README

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-4-writing-scenarios]

### Step 4: Writing Scenarios

A scenario describes one observable behavior with concrete values.

**The anatomy of a good scenario:**

```gherkin
@FR-CLK-TZ-010
Scenario: now_local converts UTC to the user configured timezone
  Given the user timezone is "America/New_York"
  And the current UTC time is "2026-06-15T18:00:00Z"
  When the system converts to local time
  Then the local time is "2026-06-15T14:00:00-04:00"
```

**Rules:**

| Rule | Rationale |
|------|-----------|
| One `When` step per scenario | Multiple `When` steps indicate multiple behaviors — split into separate scenarios |
| Concrete values, not abstractions | "America/New_York" is verifiable; "a valid timezone" is not |
| Present tense throughout | "the system converts" not "the system will convert" or "the system should convert" |
| Domain vocabulary from the glossary | Use "user timezone" if that's the glossary term, not "locale offset" |
| No implementation details in steps | "the system converts to local time" not "DateTimeOffset.ToOffset is called" |
| Scenario name describes the behavior | "now_local converts UTC to user configured timezone" — what happens, not how |

**Step keyword usage:**

| Keyword | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `Given` | Establish preconditions — the world before the action | `Given the user timezone is "America/New_York"` |
| `And` | Additional preconditions or assertions (follows Given/Then) | `And the current UTC time is "2026-06-15T18:00:00Z"` |
| `When` | The single action being tested | `When the system converts to local time` |
| `Then` | The expected outcome — what is observable after the action | `Then the local time is "2026-06-15T14:00:00-04:00"` |
| `But` | A negative assertion (follows Then) | `But no timezone conversion error is raised` |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-5-writing-scenario-outlines]

### Step 5: Writing Scenario Outlines

Use a Scenario Outline when multiple examples exercise the same behavior pattern with different data values. This avoids duplicating identical step structures.

```gherkin
@FR-CLK-TZ-020
Scenario Outline: now_local handles multiple US timezones correctly
  Given the user timezone is "<timezone>"
  And the current UTC time is "2026-06-15T18:00:00Z"
  When the system converts to local time
  Then the local time is "<expected_local>"

  Examples:
    | timezone           | expected_local                |
    | America/New_York   | 2026-06-15T14:00:00-04:00     |
    | America/Chicago    | 2026-06-15T13:00:00-05:00     |
    | America/Denver     | 2026-06-15T12:00:00-06:00     |
    | America/Los_Angeles| 2026-06-15T11:00:00-07:00     |
```

**When to use Scenario Outline vs. separate Scenarios:**

| Use Scenario Outline | Use Separate Scenarios |
|----------------------|------------------------|
| Same step structure, different data values | Different step structures or different behaviors |
| Boundary testing with a parameter table | Error paths that need distinct Given/Then patterns |
| The Examples table makes the coverage obvious | Each scenario has a meaningfully different name |

**Tagging rule:** The `@FR-` tag goes on the Scenario Outline, not on individual Examples rows. All rows in the Examples table share the same requirement ID — they are variations of the same behavior, not separate requirements.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-6-choosing-the-right-granularity]

### Step 6: Choosing the Right Granularity

Granularity failures are the most common `.feature` file defect. The guidance in the [BDD Lifecycle Strategy §5.0](../../../white-papers/engineering/bdd-lifecycle-strategy.md#50-granularity--what-level-should-requirements-be) provides the strategic framework. This section operationalizes it.

**The granularity test:**

Ask these three questions about each scenario:

1. **Can a product owner validate it without reading code?** If the scenario requires code knowledge to understand, it is too detailed.
2. **Can an engineer implement it without guessing?** If the expected behavior is ambiguous from the scenario alone, it is too abstract.
3. **Does it test one observable behavior?** If removing a `Then` assertion would leave a meaningful scenario, it is testing multiple behaviors.

**Granularity examples:**

| Level | Scenario | Verdict |
|-------|----------|---------|
| Too abstract | `Then the timezone conversion works correctly` | Fails test #2 — "works correctly" is unverifiable |
| Right | `Then the local time is "2026-06-15T14:00:00-04:00"` | Passes all three tests |
| Too detailed | `Then DateTimeOffset.ToOffset returns a new DateTimeOffset with offset -04:00` | Fails test #1 — product owner cannot validate this |

**File-level granularity:**

- **3–15 scenarios per `.feature` file** — fewer than 3 suggests the concern is too narrow to be its own file; more than 15 suggests the file covers multiple distinct capabilities
- **One `.feature` file per functional area within a concern** — `clock/core.feature` for basic time operations, `clock/timezone.feature` for timezone conversion, `clock/overrides.feature` for time override capabilities

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#synthetic-data-only]

#### Synthetic Data Only

`.feature` files must never contain Protected Health Information (PHI), Personally Identifiable Information (PII), or production data values. All example values must be synthetic and clearly fictional:

| Data Type | Prohibited | Use Instead |
|-----------|------------|-------------|
| Names | Real patient or user names | "Jane Doe", "Test User" |
| Email | Real email addresses | "user@example.com" |
| Phone | Real phone numbers | "555-0100" (reserved fictional range) |
| Dates | Dates from production incidents | "2026-06-15T18:00:00Z" |
| IDs | Real member IDs | "MBR-TEST-001" |
| Addresses | Real addresses | "123 Test Street, Anytown, ST 00000" |

This constraint aligns with [STD-GOV-AI-001](../../../../standards/governance/ai-development/STD-GOV-AI-001-agent-executable-work-item-specification-standard.md) PRO-005, which prohibits PHI/PII in agent-accessible content.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#ubiquitous-language]

#### Ubiquitous Language

All step text must use the project's ubiquitous language as defined in `docs/glossary.md`. Do not introduce new domain terms in a `.feature` file without first adding them to the glossary.

| Instead of... | Use... | Why |
|---------------|--------|-----|
| "locale offset" | "user timezone" | Glossary term |
| "session token" | "authentication context" | Glossary term |
| "DB record" | "audit event" | Domain language, not implementation language |
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-phrasing-consistency]

#### Step Phrasing Consistency

Consistent step phrasing enables step definition reuse across scenarios and `.feature` files. When writing steps:

- Reuse existing Given/When/Then phrasings from other `.feature` files in the same project
- Parameterize variable values with quoted strings: `Given the user timezone is "America/New_York"`
- Use the same phrasing for the same concept across all files — do not write `Given a timezone of "America/New_York"` in one file and `Given the user timezone is "America/New_York"` in another

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-8-using-the-rule-keyword]

### Step 8: Using the Rule Keyword

The `Rule:` keyword (Gherkin 6+) groups related scenarios under a named business rule within a feature file. Each Rule represents one independently testable concern discovered during Example Mapping.

**Structure:**

```gherkin
Feature: <capability>
  <description>

  Rule: <business rule name>

    @FR-<tag>
    Scenario: <variation of this rule>
      Given ...
      When ...
      Then ...

  Rule: <another business rule>

    @FR-<tag>
    Scenario: <variation of this rule>
      Given ...
      When ...
      Then ...
```

**Guidelines:**

- One Rule per independently testable business rule (discovered during Example Mapping)
- Each Rule contains 1–5 scenarios (variations: happy path, boundary, error)
- Rules do NOT cross-cut multiple concerns — if a rule spans concerns, it belongs in the owning concern's file
- The Rule name should be a plain-English statement of the business rule a domain SME can validate
- Rules provide coverage measurement: coverage = Rules with passing scenarios / total Rules
- A feature file with 3–15 scenarios typically contains 3–8 Rules

**When to use Rule:**

- Always — every feature file should organize scenarios under Rules
- The Rule keyword replaces informal comment-based grouping

**When NOT to use Rule:**

- Never skip it. A scenario without a Rule is an ungrouped scenario that lacks semantic context.
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#step-9-multi-jurisdiction-scenario-outlines]

### Step 9: Multi-Jurisdiction Scenario Outlines

For systems operating across multiple US states or jurisdictions, use `Scenario Outline` with jurisdiction-tagged `Examples` tables to parameterize the same scenario with state-specific data:

```gherkin
  Rule: New identity creates a person record

    @FR-EMPI-FD-010
    Scenario Outline: First-time feed creates person
      Given source system "<source>" is registered with feed permission
      When source system "<source>" feeds identity for "<name>" with SSN "<ssn>"
      Then a person record is created for "<name>"

      @generic
      Examples:
        | source    | name          | ssn         |
        | member-bc | Dustin Farmer | 555-12-3456 |

      @kansas
      Examples:
        | source    | name        | ssn         |
        | kees-feed | Sarah Mills | 555-78-9012 |
```

**Guidelines:**

- One `@FR-` tag per Scenario Outline (not per Examples table) — the Outline is ONE requirement
- Place jurisdiction tags (`@generic`, `@kansas`, `@ohio`) on individual Examples tables
- Always include a `@generic` Examples table that exercises core logic without state-specific behavior
- State-specific Examples tables exercise adapter or variation behavior for that jurisdiction
- Step definitions must be jurisdiction-agnostic — all variation comes from Gherkin data columns, never from fixtures
- CI filtering: `pytest -m "kansas"` runs only KS-specific examples in KS environments
- See PTN-APP-TEST-002 for the full pattern

**When to use jurisdiction Examples:**

- The same business rule applies across states but test data differs (different source systems, identifier formats, code sets)
- You need to gate CI by jurisdiction

**When NOT to use:**

- State-specific LOGIC (different business rules) — use separate Scenarios under separate Rules
- The jurisdiction tag would be on every Examples table identically (just use one table)

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#prerequisites]

### Prerequisites

Before authoring a `.feature` file:

1. **Glossary reviewed** — the domain terms you will use exist in `docs/glossary.md`
2. **Concern directory exists** — `docs/requirements/functional/<concern>/` is created with its README
3. **Concern abbreviation assigned** — the concern has an entry in the concern abbreviation table
4. **Business requirement understood** — the product owner can articulate what the system should do in domain language

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#authoring-workflow]

### Authoring Workflow

```
Step 1: Product owner identifies the business requirement
        └── Articulates in plain language what the system must do

Step 2: Product owner works with AI to draft Gherkin scenarios
        ├── AI elicits edge cases and boundary conditions
        ├── AI structures into Given/When/Then format
        ├── AI assigns @FR- tags from the concern abbreviation table
        └── AI validates completeness (happy path + error paths + boundaries)

Step 3: Product owner reviews and approves the draft
        ├── Validates business intent is correctly captured
        ├── Confirms concrete values are domain-correct
        └── Decides which edge cases are in scope vs. deferred

Step 4: Engineer reviews for technical correctness
        ├── Scenarios are implementable in all supported languages
        ├── Step phrasing is consistent with existing .feature files
        ├── @FR- tags follow the convention and are unique
        └── No PHI/PII in example values

Step 5: Engineer commits the .feature file
        ├── Target: docs/requirements/functional/<concern>/<file>.feature
        ├── Updates the concern abbreviation table if this is a new concern
        └── Syncs to language test directories per PTN-APP-TEST-001

Step 6: CI validates
        ├── Feature file sync check passes (byte-identical copies)
        └── BDD runners report new scenarios as pending (no step definitions yet)
```

### Critical Success Factors

- Product owner involvement is non-negotiable — engineers can format, but product owners own behavioral intent
- AI assists at every step but never makes authoring decisions — the product owner decides what scenarios say
- The `.feature` file is committed before implementation begins — this is the BDD discipline

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#decision-framework-when-to-create-a-new-feature-file-vs-extend-an-existing-one]

### Decision Framework: When to Create a New `.feature` File vs. Extend an Existing One

| Signal | Action |
|--------|--------|
| The new scenarios describe a behavior in an existing functional area | Add scenarios to the existing `.feature` file |
| The existing `.feature` file would exceed 15 scenarios | Create a new file within the same concern directory |
| The new scenarios describe a different functional area within the same concern | Create a new file (e.g., `clock/timezone.feature` alongside `clock/core.feature`) |
| The new scenarios describe a behavior in a different concern entirely | Create a new concern directory and `.feature` file |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#decision-framework-when-to-use-ai-assistance-vs-manual-authoring]

### Decision Framework: When to Use AI Assistance vs. Manual Authoring

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|----------------|
| Product owner is familiar with Gherkin and the concern is straightforward | Manual authoring is fine — AI adds overhead for simple cases |
| Business rules are complex with many edge cases | AI assistance strongly recommended — AI excels at eliciting boundary conditions |
| Product owner is new to Gherkin | AI assistance required — AI translates natural language to correct Gherkin syntax |
| Extending existing `.feature` files with consistent step phrasing | AI assistance recommended — AI maintains phrasing consistency across files |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#common-pitfalls-and-mitigations]

### Common Pitfalls and Mitigations

| Pitfall | Symptom | Mitigation |
|---------|---------|------------|
| Testing implementation instead of behavior | Steps reference class names, method names, or SQL queries | Review checklist: can a product owner understand every step? |
| Compound scenarios | Multiple `When` steps in one scenario | Split into separate scenarios — one `When` per scenario |
| Vague assertions | `Then it works correctly`, `Then the result is valid` | Require concrete values in every `Then` step |
| Missing error paths | Only happy-path scenarios exist | AI prompts for "What should happen when X fails?" during decomposition |
| Tag collisions | Two scenarios in different files share the same `@FR-` tag | Assign file abbreviations before writing scenarios; check for uniqueness |
| Prose-style steps | `When the user enters their timezone and clicks save and the system processes the request` | One action per step; decompose into Given/When/Then |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#example-1-simple-concern--cache-ttl]

### Example 1: Simple Concern — Cache TTL

**Context:** The product owner needs to specify cache entry time-to-live behavior.

**Concern directory:** `docs/requirements/functional/cache/`
**Concern abbreviation:** `CCH`
**File:** `ttl.feature`
**File abbreviation:** `TTL`

```gherkin
@cache
Feature: Cache entry time-to-live
  Cache entries expire after their configured TTL. Expired entries are not
  returned to callers, and the system treats an expired entry identically
  to a cache miss.

  @FR-CCH-TTL-010
  Scenario: Cache entry is retrievable before TTL expires
    Given a cache entry with key "user:123:profile" and TTL 30 seconds
    And the entry was set 29 seconds ago
    When the cache is queried for key "user:123:profile"
    Then the cached value is returned

  @FR-CCH-TTL-020
  Scenario: Cache entry is absent after TTL expires
    Given a cache entry with key "user:123:profile" and TTL 30 seconds
    And the entry was set 31 seconds ago
    When the cache is queried for key "user:123:profile"
    Then a cache miss is returned

  @FR-CCH-TTL-030
  Scenario: Cache entry with zero TTL is never cached
    Given a cache entry with key "user:123:profile" and TTL 0 seconds
    When the cache is queried for key "user:123:profile"
    Then a cache miss is returned
```

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#example-2-complex-concern--validation-with-scenario-outline]

### Example 2: Complex Concern — Validation with Scenario Outline

**Context:** Input validation for member enrollment with multiple field rules.

**Concern directory:** `docs/requirements/functional/validation/`
**Concern abbreviation:** `VLD`
**File:** `enrollment.feature`
**File abbreviation:** `ENR`

```gherkin
@validation
Feature: Member enrollment input validation
  All enrollment submissions are validated before processing. Invalid
  submissions return specific error codes that identify the failing field
  and the validation rule that was violated.

  @FR-VLD-ENR-010
  Scenario: Valid enrollment submission is accepted
    Given a complete enrollment submission with all required fields
    When the submission is validated
    Then the validation result is "valid"
    And no validation errors are returned

  @FR-VLD-ENR-020
  Scenario Outline: Required field validation rejects missing fields
    Given an enrollment submission missing the "<field>" field
    When the submission is validated
    Then the validation result is "invalid"
    And the error code is "<error_code>"

    Examples:
      | field        | error_code        |
      | email        | EMAIL_REQUIRED    |
      | dateOfBirth  | DOB_REQUIRED      |
      | lastName     | LASTNAME_REQUIRED |
      | stateCode    | STATE_REQUIRED    |

  @FR-VLD-ENR-030
  Scenario: Email format validation rejects malformed addresses
    Given an enrollment submission with email "not-an-email"
    When the submission is validated
    Then the validation result is "invalid"
    And the error code is "EMAIL_FORMAT_INVALID"
```

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#example-3-error-path-coverage]

### Example 3: Error Path Coverage

**Context:** Resilience concern — circuit breaker behavior.

```gherkin
@resilience
Feature: Circuit breaker state transitions
  The circuit breaker protects downstream services from cascading failures
  by transitioning through closed, open, and half-open states based on
  failure thresholds and recovery probes.

  @FR-RST-CB-010
  Scenario: Circuit breaker opens after failure threshold is reached
    Given the circuit breaker is in "closed" state
    And the failure threshold is 5 consecutive failures
    When 5 consecutive requests fail
    Then the circuit breaker transitions to "open" state

  @FR-RST-CB-020
  Scenario: Open circuit breaker rejects requests immediately
    Given the circuit breaker is in "open" state
    When a request is made
    Then the request is rejected with error "CIRCUIT_OPEN"
    But no call is made to the downstream service

  @FR-RST-CB-030
  Scenario: Circuit breaker transitions to half-open after recovery timeout
    Given the circuit breaker is in "open" state
    And the recovery timeout is 60 seconds
    When 60 seconds have elapsed since the circuit opened
    Then the circuit breaker transitions to "half-open" state

  @FR-RST-CB-040
  Scenario: Successful probe in half-open state closes the circuit
    Given the circuit breaker is in "half-open" state
    When a probe request succeeds
    Then the circuit breaker transitions to "closed" state
    And the failure counter is reset to 0

  @FR-RST-CB-050
  Scenario: Failed probe in half-open state reopens the circuit
    Given the circuit breaker is in "half-open" state
    When a probe request fails
    Then the circuit breaker transitions to "open" state
```

### Quality Gate: Feature File Review Checklist

Before a `.feature` file is committed, the reviewing engineer validates:

- [ ] Every scenario has a unique `@FR-{CONCERN}-{FILE}-{NNN}` tag
- [ ] Tag format follows the convention (correct concern abbreviation, gap numbering by 10)
- [ ] No duplicate `@FR-` tags exist across the project
- [ ] The concern abbreviation table entry exists in `docs/requirements/functional/README.md`
- [ ] Feature description explains business intent, not implementation
- [ ] Every scenario has exactly one `When` step
- [ ] All `Then` steps use concrete, verifiable values
- [ ] No step references implementation details (class names, method calls, SQL, API paths)
- [ ] All example data is synthetic — no PHI, PII, or production values
- [ ] Step phrasing is consistent with existing `.feature` files in the project
- [ ] Domain vocabulary matches `docs/glossary.md`
- [ ] Scenario count is 3–15 per file

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#traceability-integration]

### Traceability Integration

Each `@FR-` tag represents a row in the project's traceability matrix (`docs/requirements/traceability.md`). When a new `.feature` file is committed, the traceability matrix must be updated to map each `@FR-` ID to:

- The parent requirement category (functional, non-functional, business rule)
- The ADO User Story that governs it (`WI#` or `AB#` reference)
- The implementation status (pending, in-progress, implemented, verified)

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md#compliance-with-agent-pipeline-standards]

### Compliance with Agent Pipeline Standards

When `.feature` file scenarios are used as acceptance criteria in agent-executable task specs (per [PTN-APP-GOV-006](../../../../patterns/application/governance/PTN-APP-GOV-006-bdd-scenario-agent-acceptance-criteria-pattern.md)):

- The `@FR-` tag must resolve to a committed, immutable `.feature` file in the repository
- The pipeline resolves `@FR-` references to inject the full Gherkin scenario text into the agent's context
- Scenarios referenced in the spec must exist in the repository at the time the spec is triggered — referencing scenarios from an uncommitted draft is a validation failure

### Maturity Assessment

| Level | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Level 1 — Ad hoc** | Engineers write `.feature` files after implementation; no `@FR-` tagging; product owners not involved |
| **Level 2 — Establishing** | `.feature` files authored before implementation; `@FR-` tags assigned; product owners review but don't author |
| **Level 3 — Practicing** | Product owners co-author scenarios with AI assistance; `@FR-` tags used as agent acceptance criteria; polyglot sync in place |
| **Level 4 — Optimizing** | Automated quality gates enforce all conventions; traceability matrix auto-generated from `@FR-` tags; cross-project concern sharing via Golden Path templates |
